clue.text: Appeared eccentric, possibly, to European

parts.note: a cam is one kind of eccentric, an off-centre wheel or disc in machinery, hence 'possibly'

explanation.surface: Someone struck a fellow European as rather odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentric' looks like an adjective describing a person, but here it is the engineering noun: an off-centre rotating part, of which the cam is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Came and appeared are both past tenses meaning turned up or arrived on the scene.

clue.text: Sailor in hammock is famous explorer

indicators.note: in places the sailor inside the bed

parts.note: a cot is a kind of hanging bed or hammock on a ship
AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor

explanation.surface: A seaman resting in his hammock turns out to be a great explorer.
explanation.walkthrough: On board ship a cot is a swinging bed like a hammock.
explanation.definitionFit: John Cabot was the Venetian navigator who reached North America for England in 1497.

clue.text: Pathetic musical loses less when split in two parts

indicators.note: loses means letters are removed from the show's title
the letters removed are not together but in two groups, three at the front and one at the end

parts.note: Les Misérables is a famous stage musical
taken as written, the four letters to remove

explanation.surface: A sad musical gets shorter by being cut into two parts.
explanation.walkthrough: From LES MISERABLES take LES from the front and S from the end, the letters of 'less' split in two.
explanation.definitionFit: Miserable and pathetic both describe something wretched or pitiful.

clue.text: Spoke at length about fine, prepared for tearing off a strip

definitions.text: prepared for tearing off a strip

indicators.note: about means going round, so one piece is wrapped around the other here

parts.note: to perorate is to make a long, grand speech, so perorated means spoke at length
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: Someone harangued listeners about a penalty, ready to tear a strip off them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tearing off a strip' suggests a telling-off, but the definition means a sheet punched with holes along a line so pieces can be torn away.
explanation.definitionFit: A perforated sheet has rows of small holes made so that a strip can be torn off neatly.

clue.text: Diner filled with calories at last, diet abandoned for festive season

indicators.note: filled with puts one piece inside the other

parts.note: a diner is one who eats, an eater

indicators.note: at last takes the final letter of calories
abandoned suggests wild, unrestrained, so the letters of diet are rearranged

explanation.surface: A diner stuffs on calories and gives up dieting over the holidays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abandoned' reads as giving up the diet, but it is the anagram signal; 'filled with' puts the final S of calories inside the diner.
explanation.definitionFit: Eastertide is the Easter season, a festival period in the Christian calendar.

clue.text: Succeeded in becoming duke

indicators.note: in puts the letter inside the other word

parts.note: becoming means suitable or fitting, fit
S is the abbreviation for succeeded in family trees

explanation.surface: Someone managed to be made a duke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duke' looks like a nobleman, but 'dukes' is old slang for fists, from rhyming slang 'Duke of York' for fork, meaning hand.
explanation.definitionFit: In slang a duke is a fist, as in 'put up your dukes'.

clue.text: Not just handling hooligan on board

parts.note: a rough is a violent, rowdy person, a hooligan
deal is pine or fir wood cut into boards

explanation.surface: A thug is being treated unfairly aboard a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On board' reads as aboard, but board is the timber DEAL, sitting under ROUGH in the down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough deal is unfair treatment, handling that is not just.

clue.text: Criminal gang finally smashed after hearing? Not quite

indicators.note: after puts the letter at the end, following the other piece
not quite means the word is cut short of its final letter

parts.note: a trial is a hearing in a court of law

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of smashed

explanation.surface: A gang is finally broken after a court hearing, though not entirely.
explanation.walkthrough: TRIAL loses its last letter, L, through 'Not quite'; D, the last of smashed, follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A triad is a Chinese criminal secret society, a gang involved in organised crime.

clue.text: Ship-breaker?

parts.note: read as a warship and also as one who wrecks things, the clue names a vessel that is itself a breaker

explanation.walkthrough: A ship-breaker is normally a scrapyard; here it is a ship that is also something that breaks, a wrecker.
explanation.definitionFit: A destroyer is a fast warship, and literally anything that destroys or breaks things.

clue.text: Queen's style is to avoid extremes

indicators.note: avoiding extremes means dropping the first and last letters of the word

parts.note: manner is a style or way of doing something

explanation.surface: A monarch's way is to keep to moderation.
explanation.walkthrough: MANNER loses its first and last letters, M and R.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne was Queen of Great Britain from 1702 to 1714, the last Stuart monarch.

clue.text: Concern at way university fails to provide degree subject

parts.note: a concern is a firm or company, a business
ST, short for street, is a way or road
an engine or a battery that fails dies

explanation.surface: Someone worries that the path through university does not lead to a proper degree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concern' reads as worry in the surface but is the commercial sense, a firm.
explanation.definitionFit: Business studies is a subject people take a degree in, covering management, accounting and commerce.

clue.text: Workers never failing to absorb good novelist

parts.note: TU, trade union, is a body of workers

indicators.note: one thing absorbing another takes it inside, so the letter goes within the other piece
failing suggests breaking down, so the letters of never are rearranged

explanation.surface: Tireless workers soak up something good from a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Failing' reads as never failing, tireless, but it is the anagram signal; 'to absorb' puts G inside the rearranged letters, right after the R.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivan Turgenev was a nineteenth-century Russian novelist, author of Fathers and Sons.

clue.text: Cloak is cleaner the same on the inside

indicators.note: on the inside places the second piece within the first

parts.note: a char, or charwoman, is a British term for a cleaning lady
DO, short for ditto, means the same as above

explanation.surface: A garment and a cleaner are said to be just alike within.
explanation.walkthrough: A CHAR is a British term for a woman paid to clean houses; DO is the abbreviation of ditto, used in lists to mean 'the same'.
explanation.definitionFit: A chador is a large cloak or shawl worn by some Muslim women covering head and body.

clue.text: A boot in high fashion

parts.note: a boot is a kick, and one sent steeply skyward for the chasers to run under is a rugby kick of this kind

explanation.surface: A trendy boot is all the rage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High fashion' suggests designer clothes, but means a kick sent high in rugby so that the kicker's side can chase it and challenge for the ball as it comes down.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby an up-and-under is a high kick, a boot that lets the chasing players get under the ball.

clue.text: Firmly establish I have a teaching qualification

parts.note: I'm can be a contraction of I am, but here it stands for I have in a loose way: the letters I'M from 'I' plus a short form
BEd, Bachelor of Education, is a teaching degree

explanation.surface: A newly qualified teacher announces their degree to secure their place.
explanation.walkthrough: IM here is the contraction I'm, read loosely as I have; BEd is the British Bachelor of Education degree held by many teachers.
explanation.definitionFit: Imbed is a variant spelling of embed, to fix something firmly in place.

clue.text: Keenly interested during tie-break

indicators.note: break means smashing the letters so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Spectators are gripped as a tennis set goes to a tie-break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tie-break' looks like one tennis term, but 'break' is the anagram signal acting on 'during tie'.
explanation.definitionFit: Intrigued means having one's curiosity or interest strongly aroused.

clue.text: Minister's answer to road blocks is in desk, unfinished

indicators.note: is in places the following pieces inside the trimmed word
unfinished means the last letter of desk is removed

parts.note: traffic cones are used to block roads

explanation.surface: A clergyman finds the solution to road closures in an unfinished desk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfinished' trims desk to DES; A plus CONES goes between its E and S.
explanation.definitionFit: A deaconess is a woman serving as a deacon, a minister in certain Christian churches.

clue.text: Part of Ireland a long way away if going by air

definitions.text: Part of Ireland a long way away if going by air

parts.words: Part of Ireland a long way away if going by air
parts.note: the old marching song says it is a long way to this Irish county, and an air is a tune, so going by the air of the song it is far off

explanation.surface: An Irish county seems remote to a traveller thinking of flying there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going by air' suggests flying, but an air is a tune: the First World War song 'It's a Long Way to Tipperary' says the county is far away.
explanation.definitionFit: Tipperary is a county in Ireland, made famous by the wartime song about it being a long way off.

clue.text: Second possible harvest at the farm failed

indicators.note: failed suggests things going wrong, so the letters of at the farm are rearranged

explanation.surface: A second crop at the farm has failed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aftermath' now means consequences, but its old sense is a second mowing of grass in the same season.
explanation.definitionFit: Aftermath originally meant a second crop of grass mown after the first harvest, math being an old word for mowing.

clue.text: Time to cut down forest to make book

parts.note: to hew is to cut down with an axe
the Forest of Arden is the woodland setting of As You Like It

explanation.surface: Felling trees to produce paper for a book takes time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' is the definition, the Trollope novel; the Forest of Arden is in Warwickshire and in Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: The Warden is an 1855 novel by Anthony Trollope, the first of his Barsetshire books.

clue.text: Eventually took food in both hands

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: L and R stand for left and right, both hands
ate means took food

explanation.surface: Someone finally ate using both hands.
explanation.walkthrough: ATE goes between L and R, the abbreviations for the left and right hands.
explanation.definitionFit: Later and eventually both mean at some time after now, in due course.

clue.text: Rate of arrival in fact halved — not high

indicators.note: halved keeps just the first half of the letters of in fact

parts.note: low is the opposite of high

explanation.surface: Arrivals are in fact down by half, nowhere near high.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Halved' keeps INF, the first three of the six letters of 'in fact'.
explanation.definitionFit: An inflow is the amount or rate of something coming in, such as water or money arriving.

clue.text: Place provided for raising temporary stage

indicators.note: in a down clue raising means the letters read upwards, so the pieces are turned backwards

parts.note: to put is to place
if means provided, on condition that

explanation.surface: A site is supplied for lifting a makeshift platform.
explanation.walkthrough: PUT plus IF read upwards gives FI TUP.
explanation.definitionFit: A fit-up is a temporary stage and scenery, as used by touring theatre companies.

clue.text: In cold weather, children go round this harbour

definitions.text: In cold weather, children go round this harbour

parts.words: In cold weather, children go round this harbour
parts.note: the nursery rhyme has children going round a bush on a cold and frosty morning, and the same plant's name was given to the floating harbours of D-Day

explanation.surface: Children circle a port on a frosty morning.
explanation.walkthrough: The British nursery rhyme 'Here we go round the mulberry bush on a cold and frosty morning' supplies the cold and the children; the Mulberry harbours were the prefabricated ports towed to Normandy in 1944.
explanation.definitionFit: Mulberry was the code name of the portable harbours built for the Allied landings in Normandy.

clue.text: This weed a nuisance

definitions.meaning: the word that goes before weed to name the climbing plant, so this word plus weed is a weed

explanation.walkthrough: Bindweed is the weed; a bind is British informal for a tiresome task.
explanation.definitionFit: Bind joined to weed names the plant, and on its own is informal British for a tedious nuisance.

clue.text: Swift chap turning up crop circles

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up reads the word upwards, backwards

parts.note: hay is a crop of grass
O is a circle, so two circles are OO

explanation.surface: A fast-moving man flips over crop circles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swift' is Jonathan Swift: in Gulliver's Travels the Yahoos are brutish humans.
explanation.definitionFit: A Yahoo is one of the brutish people in Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels, so a Swift chap.

clue.text: Island lacking a whisky

indicators.note: lacking means the letter is removed

parts.note: Malta is a Mediterranean island

explanation.surface: An island has no whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: Malt is short for malt whisky, made from malted barley.

clue.text: Where one may be mistakenly led to the stocks?

definitions.text: Where one may be mistakenly led to the stocks?

parts.words: Where one may be mistakenly led to the stocks
parts.note: being led astray is a stock idiom about a walk among flowers, and stocks are garden flowers that line such a walk

explanation.surface: A deceived person is marched off to the old wooden punishment frame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The stocks' suggests the old punishment frame, but stocks are garden flowers; to lead someone up the garden path is to deceive them.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom of leading someone along this route means misleading them, and stocks grow beside such a walk.

clue.text: Payment put down before Golden Treasury finally appears in store

parts.note: a deposit is a payment put down in advance
OR is the heraldic term for gold

indicators.note: finally picks the final letter of Treasury

explanation.surface: A down payment comes before a famous poetry anthology turns up in a shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Golden Treasury' looks like Palgrave's anthology, but splits into OR, heraldic gold, and the last letter of Treasury.
explanation.definitionFit: A depository is a place where things are stored for safekeeping, a store or warehouse.

clue.text: Cry of surprise — I plunged in great river

indicators.note: something plunged in goes inside the other piece

parts.note: oho is an exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: Someone yelps in surprise after jumping into a big river.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ohio is a major American river, a large tributary of the Mississippi.
